# Sleep Hygiene Changes for Better Evening Rest

For a healthy 34-year-old with mild seasonal allergies and no chronic conditions, the biggest wins usually come from reducing alerting cues at night and making bedtime more predictable. The ranking below balances likely sleep impact with how easy each change is to keep doing.

# Ranked Comparison of 5 Evening Habit Changes

| Rank | Change | Likely impact | Ease | Why it helps | Best first step |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Fixed wake time | High | High | Anchors the body clock and improves sleep drive the next night | Pick one wake time for all 7 days |
| 2 | 60-minute wind-down | High | High | Lowers mental and physical arousal before bed | Start a repeatable pre-bed routine |
| 3 | Reduce evening light/screens | High | Medium | Bright light can delay melatonin and make it harder to fall asleep | Dim lights and stop scrolling 30–60 min before bed |
| 4 | Cut caffeine after early afternoon | Medium-high | High | Caffeine can still be active at bedtime and fragment sleep | Set a caffeine cutoff time |
| 5 | Make the bedroom cooler, darker, quieter | Medium | Medium | Sleep tends to be easier in a calm, cool environment | Adjust temperature, blackout, and noise control |

## Best-Evidence Sleep Hygiene Changes

### 1) Keep the same wake time every day
- **Why it ranks first:** This is one of the strongest ways to stabilize circadian rhythm.
- **What to do:** Choose a wake time you can keep on weekdays and weekends.
- **Good sign it’s working:** Falling asleep becomes easier after several days, even if bedtime varies a little.
- **Trade-off:** Social plans may make this harder, but it usually pays off fastest.

### 2) Build a 60-minute wind-down
- **Why it matters:** A predictable routine tells your brain the day is ending.
- **What to do:** Use the same sequence each night, such as shower, prep clothes, light reading, and brushing teeth.
- **Best for:** People whose minds stay “on” at night.
- **Trade-off:** It requires consistency more than effort.

### 3) Lower light and screen stimulation before bed
- **Why it matters:** Bright light and engaging content can delay sleepiness.
- **What to do:** Dim overhead lights and avoid high-stimulation scrolling or work in the last hour.
- **Best for:** Late-night screen users.
- **Trade-off:** Easier to do partially than perfectly, so even a 30-minute reduction helps.

### 4) Stop caffeine earlier in the day
- **Why it matters:** Caffeine can reduce sleep quality even when you feel “used to it.”
- **What to do:** Set a cutoff around early afternoon, especially if you are sensitive.
- **Best for:** Coffee, tea, energy drink, and pre-workout users.
- **Trade-off:** If you rely on late caffeine, the first few days may feel harder.

### 5) Optimize the sleep environment
- **Why it matters:** A cooler, darker, quieter room reduces awakenings and helps sleep continuity.
- **What to do:** Lower temperature, use blackout curtains or an eye mask, and reduce noise.
- **Best for:** Light sleepers and people with seasonal allergy-related congestion.
- **Trade-off:** Helpful, but usually less powerful than circadian and routine changes.

## 2-Week Sleep Experiment Plan

### Week 1: Stabilize the clock
- **Days 1-3:** Set a fixed wake time; keep it every day.
- **Days 1-7:** Start a 60-minute wind-down.
- **Days 1-7:** Move caffeine cutoff earlier.
- **Track each morning:** bedtime, time to fall asleep, number of awakenings, and how rested you feel.

### Week 2: Reduce sleep friction
- **Days 8-14:** Keep the same wake time and wind-down.
- **Days 8-14:** Reduce evening light/screens more aggressively.
- **Days 8-14:** Improve the room setup for coolness, darkness, and quiet.
- **Compare to Week 1:** Look for faster sleep onset, fewer awakenings, and better morning alertness.

### Simple scoring method
- Rate each morning from **1 to 5** for:
  - Sleep quality
  - Morning energy
  - Ease of falling asleep
- At the end of 2 weeks, keep the 2–3 changes with the best scores and easiest adherence.
